frictionVectors.title: European Energy Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control over hydrocarbons through Sonatrach, but European buyers and shifting gas markets constrain pricing and investment choices.

frictionVectors.title: Southern Border Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Libya, and Niger increases security costs and tests Algeria's non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Finance
frictionVectors.details: Angola is diversifying partnerships beyond China, but debt servicing, oil-backed obligations, and foreign control of major infrastructure remain significant constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Corridor Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor is attracting U.S., European, and Chinese interest, creating opportunities for Angola while intensifying competition over logistics and mineral access.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Border and Pipeline Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Relations with Niger remain vulnerable to sanctions legacies, border insecurity, and disputes affecting the oil-export corridor and regional trade.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Linked Logistics Growth
frictionVectors.details: Port and transport expansion can strengthen Benin's sovereignty, but reliance on external operators, financiers, and regional commerce leaves infrastructure exposed to outside leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains unusually strong leverage over diamond value capture, but weaker global demand and synthetic stones challenge the fiscal model.

frictionVectors.title: Diversification Execution
frictionVectors.details: Efforts to develop copper, rare-earth, solar, and processing industries could improve sovereignty, though capital and technical dependence remain substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Control and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater state control and domestic processing of gold, but foreign firms, informal mining networks, and weak regulatory capacity complicate implementation.

frictionVectors.title: Security Corridor Breakdown
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist attacks threaten mining zones, transport routes, and state revenue, while reliance on Russian-linked security assistance creates a new form of external dependence.

highlights: China and regional partners deepen infrastructure ties

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater control over nickel, rare-earth, and other mineral projects, but limited regulatory capacity and opaque contracting leave room for foreign leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security dependence
frictionVectors.details: Burundi remains economically and diplomatically exposed to aid conditions and tensions with Rwanda, constraining its room for independent resource and security policy.

highlights: Tourism and external finance remain decisive

frictionVectors.title: Port and connectivity competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde is leveraging its ports, air links, and maritime position, while foreign investors and partners compete for influence over logistics and digital infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Water and energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported fuel, desalination, food, and climate-sensitive infrastructure limits practical sovereignty despite strong institutions and diversified international partnerships.

highlights: Oil and gas leverage remains state-centered

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and pipeline risk
frictionVectors.details: Insurgency in the Northwest and Southwest continues to undermine territorial control and threatens transport corridors linking productive zones to ports and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-backed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese construction and financing remain central to roads, energy, and public works, creating debt, procurement, and strategic-dependence concerns alongside Western and Gulf engagement.

frictionVectors.title: Russian security-for-access model
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel provide regime protection while retaining strong influence around mining and commercial interests, limiting transparent state control over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-group territorial control
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks still contest transport routes and resource zones, making formal concessions difficult to enforce and increasing dependence on external security actors.

highlights: Oil finances a tightly centralized state

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues remain the core fiscal resource, while foreign operators, export infrastructure, and volatile prices constrain the state's effective control over its resource base.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan-border destabilization
frictionVectors.details: War and displacement from Sudan place heavy pressure on eastern Chad, diverting resources toward security and humanitarian management and increasing reliance on international support.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a core sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' effective authority over surrounding maritime space. The issue also drives migration tensions and periodic diplomatic friction.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external financing and technical support for ports, energy, telecommunications, and transport. Gulf, Turkish, French, and other partners compete for influence without yet establishing decisive control.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and Regional Intervention
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in eastern Congo continues to weaken state authority over territory, transport corridors, and mining zones, with Rwanda and other regional actors central to the security dispute. Displacement and contested border trade further erode sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Minerals Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Cobalt, copper, gold, and coltan attract intense competition among Chinese, Western, and regional firms. The state is seeking better terms and greater processing capacity, but weak enforcement and opaque concessions continue to limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon Revenue Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to fiscal stability and export earnings, leaving national strategy vulnerable to price shifts and foreign technical and commercial partners. Limited diversification constrains the state's bargaining power over resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, rail, and port projects have expanded connectivity but increased concerns over debt service, project transparency, and strategic dependence. Competition among Chinese, French, and other investors is widening Congo's options without removing structural vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa and Commodity Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is strengthening domestic processing and state oversight, but farmers and public finances remain exposed to volatile cocoa prices and the market power of international traders. Climate stress and supply-chain compliance requirements add pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan and San Pedro are attracting major foreign investment in ports, logistics, gas, and offshore oil. The government retains meaningful negotiating capacity, but French, Chinese, Gulf, and other external interests compete for long-term infrastructure influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its location through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, gaining revenue and diplomatic weight while accepting constraints on strategic autonomy. Rivalry among external powers raises the value and risk of the corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port and rail infrastructure tied to Ethiopia and international shipping is vital to the economy, but debt exposure and dependence on foreign operators narrow policy flexibility. Competition between Chinese-linked assets and Western and Gulf alternatives is intensifying.

frictionVectors.title: GERD Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt remains locked in a strategic dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam and Nile flows. Cairo is seeking binding operating guarantees while avoiding escalation that could damage regional trade and diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gulf investment, IMF programs, and foreign currency inflows are supporting Egypt's infrastructure and balance of payments. These arrangements increase outside leverage over strategic assets and economic policy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining mature oil fields are increasing pressure to attract foreign technology and capital for offshore gas and LNG projects. The state retains formal control, but production and revenue remain dependent on external operators.

frictionVectors.title: China-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed ports, roads, and public works remain central to the country's infrastructure model. Debt opacity and weak utilization create long-term risks of strategic dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's Red Sea coastline gives it strategic value amid competition involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, Egypt, and other maritime actors. External pressure over port access could challenge Asmara's insistence on tightly controlled sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Partnership Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc projects depend heavily on foreign firms and external logistics. Limited transparency and sanctions-related constraints complicate the state's ability to convert mineral assets into broad-based national capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's trade, energy, transport, and fiscal stability remain deeply tied to South Africa and the Southern African Customs Union. This limits independent control over critical supply chains and revenue policy.

frictionVectors.title: Agricultural Resource Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Sugar exports and irrigated agriculture depend on reliable water and cross-border markets. Drought risk, land concentration, and infrastructure dependence expose the sector to external shocks and political contestation.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia's electricity and bargaining position but continues to drive confrontation with Egypt and tensions with Sudan. Disputes over filling, drought management, and data sharing remain unresolved.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, Turkish, and multilateral financing supports power, transport, and industrial infrastructure while increasing exposure to debt restructuring and external conditions. Addis Ababa is attempting to diversify partners and retain control of strategic corridors.

highlights: Post-transition government consolidates control over oil and mining

frictionVectors.title: Mining Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Libreville is seeking greater state participation and local processing in manganese, iron ore, and timber. Tighter terms could unsettle established foreign operators and delay investment.

frictionVectors.title: China-France Competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese infrastructure and mining finance is expanding while French commercial influence remains significant. The government is balancing diversification against debt and project-execution risks.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty rests on Senegalese security and trade links
Fisheries and tourism remain vulnerable to external capture

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing and weak monitoring threaten coastal livelihoods and state revenue. Limited enforcement capacity leaves room for foreign fleets and opaque licensing arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal Dependency
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for regional logistics, energy connectivity, and security cooperation. This provides stability but narrows Banjul's room for independent infrastructure and trade policy.

highlights: State seeks stronger control over gold and lithium value chains
Debt pressure constrains resource-led industrial policy

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Formalization
frictionVectors.details: Accra is consolidating gold purchasing and export channels to capture more value and curb smuggling. Resistance from informal networks, foreign buyers, and entrenched commercial interests remains substantial.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Mining and Lithium Terms
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining is damaging water systems and undermining state authority, while lithium development raises demands for local processing and transparent contracts. Fiscal dependence on external capital limits negotiating leverage.

highlights: Junta uses Simandou to anchor a resource-nationalist development model
Bauxite and iron ore exports deepen infrastructure dependence

frictionVectors.title: Simandou External Leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron ore corridor is financed and operated through complex foreign partnerships, making rail, port, and revenue arrangements central sovereignty concerns. The project could transform state capacity but also lock Guinea into long-term external dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Political Closure
frictionVectors.details: The military government limits political competition while accelerating mining commitments. Weak public oversight increases the risk that resource gains accrue to contractors and elites rather than broad-based development.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed to external buyers
Political instability weakens control over ports and natural resources

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Value-Chain Capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign traders and processors capture much of the value from the country's dominant export, while limited domestic processing reduces bargaining power. Price swings and opaque licensing directly affect fiscal and rural stability.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Security Influence
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political crises create openings for external actors to shape port access, security relationships, and commercial concessions. This constrains Bissau's ability to set a coherent sovereign infrastructure strategy.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya remains reliant on IMF support, commercial creditors, and Chinese-linked infrastructure finance, limiting policy autonomy over fiscal and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and Lamu face overlapping Gulf, Chinese, and Western commercial interests as Kenya seeks to control regional logistics and energy routes.

frictionVectors.title: Dependence on South African Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports and electricity access remain structurally tied to South Africa, giving Pretoria significant leverage over national resource strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project brings vital revenue and infrastructure but leaves the country exposed to financing, construction, and governance risks involving foreign contractors.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore and Port Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-controlled mining and rail-port systems remain central to Liberia's exports, constraining domestic value capture and exposing Monrovia to investor pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Governance Reform
frictionVectors.details: The government faces pressure to renegotiate concession terms and improve transparency while preserving investment in mining, rubber, forestry, and port infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Oil Authorities
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security networks continue to contest control over oil revenues, production facilities, and export decisions, weakening unified sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Patronage
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked actors, Egypt, the UAE, and European states retain influence through military, political, and energy relationships that constrain Libya's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Large nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mining projects are dominated by foreign capital, while Madagascar continues to struggle to secure stronger domestic processing and fiscal returns.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Weak electricity and transport networks increase reliance on foreign developers and donors, giving external actors leverage over strategic corridors and resource projects.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Governance and Foreign Capital
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking investment in uranium, rare earths and other minerals, but weak fiscal capacity limits its ability to secure favorable terms. Contract transparency and local value capture remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Power Import and Grid Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Chronic electricity shortages and dependence on imported fuel and fertilizer constrain industrial autonomy. External lenders and development partners remain pivotal to infrastructure stabilization.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Concessions and Barrick Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is asserting greater state control over gold revenues and has confronted major foreign operators over taxes, permits and ownership. The dispute risks reducing investment while strengthening the junta's resource-nationalist posture.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Influence
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has displaced much Western and regional involvement, but the relationship creates opacity around payments, concessions and strategic infrastructure. Insecurity continues to limit effective national control outside major urban centers.

frictionVectors.title: Greater Tortue Ahmeyim Revenue and Control
frictionVectors.details: The offshore gas project with Senegal offers Mauritania new fiscal and diplomatic leverage, while foreign operators retain decisive control over technology, financing and marketing. Revenue management will determine whether gas strengthens or deepens dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Transport Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports and planned green-hydrogen projects depend heavily on foreign capital, port capacity and long-distance transport links. Chinese, Gulf and European interests are competing for access to these sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Negotiations
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues to pursue recognition of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while balancing relations with the United Kingdom, United States and India. The military-base question makes the issue strategically sensitive despite Mauritius's diplomatic leverage.

frictionVectors.title: External Financial and Maritime Dependence
frictionVectors.details: International scrutiny of offshore finance and dependence on imported energy constrain policy autonomy. Mauritius is attempting to convert its port, fisheries and blue-economy assets into more sovereign sources of growth.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Investment Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is consolidating infrastructure and economic activity in Western Sahara while seeking wider international recognition of its position. Algeria and the Polisario Front remain major strategic obstacles, with external investors exposed to legal and diplomatic risk.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Tanger Med, renewable energy, electric-vehicle supply chains and green-hydrogen plans expand Moroccan leverage but rely on European, Gulf and Chinese finance and technology. Water scarcity and energy-import exposure remain structural constraints on sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Led LNG Security
frictionVectors.details: Major gas projects depend on international security assistance and foreign operators, limiting Maputo's control over the pace and terms of development.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity in Cabo Delgado continues to threaten communities, transport corridors, and the state's ability to secure strategic energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital in New Energy
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil, uranium, and green-hydrogen projects are attracting major external investors, creating pressure to preserve local value capture and fiscal leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Export Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large energy projects depend on scarce water and expanded ports, power networks, and rail links, exposing Namibia to financing and offtake pressures from foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Rebalancing
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater control over uranium and other mineral assets while renegotiating relationships with Western firms, raising investment and production risks.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Reduced Western engagement has increased reliance on Russian-linked security support, trading strategic autonomy for new external dependence and uncertain accountability.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Delta Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, vandalism, and local grievances continue to weaken state control over production corridors and reduce the public return from petroleum assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Refining Politics
frictionVectors.details: Nigeria needs international finance and technical partners, but emerging domestic refining capacity is strengthening bargaining power over crude supply, fuel imports, and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral and Security Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern DRC generate sustained diplomatic pressure and threaten access to Western financing.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The state retains strong domestic control, but development finance, technology imports, and regional logistics remain exposed to conditionality from external partners.

frictionVectors.title: OFFSHORE EXPLORATION TERMS
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is seeking credible offshore petroleum investment while protecting fiscal terms and avoiding overreliance on foreign operators. Limited state capacity and uncertain discoveries constrain bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL FINANCING DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Portugal, China, Gulf-linked actors, and multilateral lenders remain important to infrastructure and budget support. This gives partners influence over strategic projects despite the country's efforts to diversify.

highlights: Oil and gas sovereignty agenda advances

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON CONTRACT REVIEW
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater domestic value capture and more scrutiny of legacy oil and gas agreements, including the Sangomar and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim projects. Renegotiation pressure could improve state control but unsettle operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's strategic port and transport infrastructure attract strong Gulf, European, Chinese, and Turkish interest. Managing concessions while expanding local participation is central to Senegal's economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles relies on external partners, including India, France, and other maritime powers, for surveillance, patrol capacity, and anti-trafficking operations. These partnerships protect vital waters but create continuing sovereignty sensitivities.

frictionVectors.title: TOURISM AND INFRASTRUCTURE FINANCE
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital dominates major tourism, airport, port, and energy investments. The government is trying to preserve environmental and economic control while remaining dependent on outside financing and imported fuel.

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINERAL CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore, rutile, and other mining operations remain central to exports but expose Sierra Leone to foreign corporate leverage and commodity-price volatility. Weak local processing and revenue constraints limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed investment in ports, roads, energy, and mining corridors is essential to growth but can embed long-term concession and repayment obligations. Freetown faces pressure to balance Chinese, Middle Eastern, and Western interests.

frictionVectors.title: TURKEY AND GULF SECURITY FOOTPRINT
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, and other partners provide military, port, and economic support that strengthens federal capacity but gives external actors influence over strategic infrastructure. Mogadishu is balancing this support against concerns about fragmented national sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: SOMALILAND AND RED SEA ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: The dispute over Somaliland's status and external access arrangements around Berbera continues to complicate Somalia's territorial claims and regional diplomacy. Red Sea competition increases the strategic value of Somali ports while amplifying pressure from neighboring and Gulf powers.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is seeking greater domestic beneficiation and local control over platinum-group metals, manganese, and rare-earth supply chains. Chinese, European, and U.S. competition for strategic minerals limits Pretoria's room to impose restrictive terms.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and freight bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Eskom's financial and generation constraints, together with rail and port failures, continue to weaken industrial sovereignty. Private capital and foreign technical support are filling gaps, but often without resolving structural state-capacity problems.

frictionVectors.title: Oil transit dependency
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's export economy depends on pipelines and refineries crossing conflict-affected Sudan, leaving production and public revenue exposed to external political leverage. International operators retain substantial influence over technical capacity and export access.

frictionVectors.title: Armed control of infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Political and military factions continue to compete over oil facilities, roads, and border corridors. Weak institutions and fragmented security arrangements allow external commercial and regional actors to negotiate access through competing power centers.

highlights: Red Sea access is strategic prize

frictionVectors.title: Gold and war financing
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling remain central to financing rival armed networks, with foreign buyers and regional intermediaries shaping access to mining zones and export routes. This diverts resource wealth away from national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, roads, and Red Sea logistics has become both a military objective and an arena for outside influence. Gulf, Egyptian, Russian, and other regional interests compete for security and commercial leverage while the state remains divided.

highlights: Mining rules seek stronger state returns

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail concessions
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam port and major rail projects are attracting Gulf, Chinese, Turkish, and other foreign capital. The government is gaining connectivity and bargaining power, but long-term concessions could create dependence if transparency and local-value requirements remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is tightening oversight of gold, graphite, nickel, and rare-earth projects to capture more revenue and processing capacity. Investor pressure and competition among external partners may test the government's ability to enforce local-content and environmental rules.

frictionVectors.title: Port-centered external leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a major national asset and a gateway to landlocked West African markets, but its expansion relies heavily on foreign finance, operators, and shipping networks. Disruptions or shifts in regional security can quickly affect sovereign revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate remains strategically important, yet limited downstream processing reduces domestic value capture. Foreign technology, finance, and market access continue to shape production while environmental and labor pressures constrain state legitimacy.

highlights: EU migration leverage meets fiscal dependence
Phosphate and energy sovereignty remain constrained

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European funding and market access remain linked to migration management, limiting Tunisian policy autonomy. Fiscal stress also keeps the country exposed to external lenders and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Heavy dependence on imported hydrocarbons and intermittent domestic production constrains Tunisia's economic sovereignty. Renewable investment is growing but has not yet materially reduced exposure.

highlights: Oil corridor advances amid sovereignty disputes
China anchors infrastructure and debt exposure

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and environmental backlash
frictionVectors.details: The Uganda-Tanzania oil pipeline offers export revenue but leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, lenders, and transit arrangements. Land acquisition and environmental concerns continue to generate international pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-finance dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign contractors remain central to major transport and energy projects. Debt service and project terms can narrow Kampala's room to maximize domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Western, Chinese, and Gulf investors to seek better terms for copper and cobalt development. Processing capacity and contract enforcement remain weaker than the country's resource position.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and power-system constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms have stabilized access to financing but restrict short-term policy flexibility. Electricity shortages threaten mining output and increase reliance on external investment in generation and transmission.

highlights: Lithium ambitions confront foreign capital dominance

frictionVectors.title: Opaque mining concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms remain central to lithium, platinum, gold, and diamond extraction, while opaque licensing and limited local processing constrain domestic value capture. Policy reversals and export controls have increased investor and sovereignty tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Sanctions, restricted access to international finance, and currency instability push Harare toward selective reliance on Chinese, Gulf, and regional partners. This diversifies diplomatic options but can weaken transparency and bargaining power.
